recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say which rule shortens the work, and what the ordered pairs look like at the end.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Use the rule (A × B) ∩ (A × C) = A × (B ∩ C)
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write the rule, then the one small intersection it leaves you with.
lines: For any three sets, (A × B) ∩ (A × C) = A × (B ∩ C).

recall.must_convey: That (A × B) ∩ (A × C) = A × (B ∩ C) and that B ∩ C = {3}.
accept: the first set is common so it becomes A times B intersection C
use the rule A cross B cap A cross C equals A cross B cap C
B intersection C is just three
A common ga undi kabatti B cap C matrame teesukovali
intersect B and C first, that gives the set three

steps.why: A × B has 6 pairs and A × C has 9, so listing both and comparing them is slow. The rule replaces that with one intersection of two small sets, because the first set A is shared by both products.
common_mistakes: Using B ∪ C in place of B ∩ C, which gives far too many pairs.
Listing A × B and A × C and then writing their union instead of the pairs common to both.
steps.memory_tip: A is the first set in both products, so only the second sets are intersected: keep A, intersect B and C.

steps.label: Write out the ordered pairs
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The answer is a set of ordered pairs, so every member is written with brackets and a comma.
lines: The first member of each pair comes from A and the second is 3.

recall.must_convey: That A × {3} gives the three pairs (1, 3), (2, 3) and (3, 3).
accept: A cross the set three gives one three two three and three three
the first coordinate runs over A and the second is always three
A lo prathi member tho three ni jodinchali
the answer is the set of pairs one three two three three three

steps.why: In A × X the first coordinate always comes from A and the second from X, so with X = {3} there are n(A) × 1 = 3 pairs. Checking the two products directly gives the same three pairs.
common_mistakes: Writing the pairs the other way round, as (3, 1), (3, 2), (3, 3).
Giving the answer as the set of numbers {1, 2, 3} instead of a set of ordered pairs.
Writing A × {3} as {1, 2, 3, 3} and treating it as an ordinary set.
steps.memory_tip: In a cross product the first coordinate comes from the left set and the second from the right set, always in that order.
